title: Diabetes Mellitus
body: Diabetes Mellitus is a chronic metabolic disease, characterised by persistent hyperglycaemia.

title: c-m1-02-02
instruction: Select the pictures below to learn more.

frontImage.alt: Woman checking her blood sugar level with a glucometer

_items.backBody: Hyperglycaemia can be brought on by resistance to the peripheral effects of insulin, decreased insulin production, or both.
Chronic hyperglycaemia combined with other metabolic abnormalities can harm multiple organ systems and result in life-threatening and incapacitating health complications.

frontImage.alt: Blood sample with diabetes test results

_items.backBody: Diabetes is a more heterogeneous disease than the classic subdivision into type 1 and type 2 diabetes and includes a third classification called latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (LADA), a common but understudied form of diabetes with features of both type 1 and type 2 diabetes.

title: Pathophysiology
instruction: Select the pictures below until you have seen all the information for each category.

_items.body: Type 1 DM is characterised by insulin deficiency which is caused by autoreactive T-cells of the immune system that destroy the pancreatic beta-cells.
The autoimmune reaction leads to a progressive loss of functional beta-cell mass and declining insulin production.
Pathogenesis of T1DM
Typically, T2DM is preceded by prediabetes.
Prediabetes is characterised by raised blood glucose levels (fasting plasma glucose levels of 6.1–6.9 mmol/L and two-hours post glucose ingestion levels between 7.8–11 mmol/L).
These changes occur due to declining islet beta-cell mass and function (usually over a few years) but not enough to warrant a diagnosis of T2DM.
Patients with prediabetes are asymptomatic but ~5–10 % progress to T2DM each year.
Type 2 DM are characterised by insulin resistance in skeletal muscle, liver and adipose tissue, together with impaired insulin secretion.
Insulin resistance reduces peripheral glucose uptake and stimulates hepatic glucose output, leading to elevated blood glucose levels.

Hyperglycaemia increases the demand on the beta-cells for a compensatory rise in insulin secretion, which may consequently exhaust the beta-cells and lead to a progressive loss of beta-cell function, leading to insulin deficiency and subsequent diabetes.

In healthy individuals:
  • insulin is produced and secreted by beta-cells in the islets of Langerhans when blood glucose levels are high.
  • Insulin binds to the insulin receptor (IR), which allows uptake of glucose into tissues to be catabolised in the cell for ATP production, which provides the fuel for intracellular processes, or converted to either glycogen or fat for fuel storage after uptake.

In individuals with T2D:
  • beta-cells have impaired function which results in markedly reduced insulin levels in circulation, while insulin resistance of the peripheral tissue impairs the action of insulin, resulting in reduced uptake of glucose from circulation.
  • Inappropriate glucagon secretion, diminished incretin hormone action, increased proinsulin secretion, impaired pancreatic islet neural regulation, and islet amyloid deposition are all characteristic of T2D.
  • The incretin effect is greatly diminished in T2D where GLP-1 and GIP account for <20 % of the insulin release after glucose ingestion in patients, believed to be due to dysfunctional beta-cells.
Pathogenesis of T2DM
Similar to T1DM, LADA patients display autoantibodies which is indicative of an autoimmune pathogenesis, but this effect seems to be milder and the progression of beta-cell failure slower.
LADA patients consistently display higher levels of C-peptide as indicator of insulin secretion and do not require insulin for some time following diagnosis.
Compared to patients with T2DM, those with LADA have less insulin secretion and progress to insulin dependence faster.
LADA patients tend to be positive primarily for Glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies (GADA), which can be used as a measure to use for LADA diagnosis.

title: Aetiology
instruction: Select the headings below to learn more.

_items.body: Both T1DM and T2DM are strongly associated with genetic factors.
Family history of diabetes increased the risk of LADA six-fold in individuals with family history of T1DM compared to 2-fold in those with family history of T2DM.

_graphic.alt: Doctor holding a 3D render of DNA

_items.body: The impact on the development of T1DM of virus exposure, lifestyle choices, weight gain and psychological stress has been difficult to map.

T2DM has been linked to a number of factors.
  • Excess weight is the strongest risk factor; obesity is associated with a seven-fold increased risk.
  • Sedentary time and hours of TV viewing is positively associated with incidence of T2DM, while physical activity is associated with a reduced risk.
  • Smokers have excess risk that increases in a dose-response manner by number of cigarettes.
  • Diet choices (regardless of BMI) has shown to impact risk. T2DM risk is reduced by diets rich in whole grain, fruit and vegetables, alcohol (moderate vs. no intake) and coffee. An increased risk is associated with consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages, red and processed meat.

title: Diagnostic factors
body:
Diabetes Mellitus is diagnosed based on A1C and plasma glucose.

Plasma glucose criteria include:
  • Fasting plasma glucose.
  • 2-h plasma glucose during glucose tolerance test (OGTT).
  • Random glucose accompanied by classic symptoms.
If T1DM is suspected, an islet autoantibody and C-peptide test should be performed.

title: c-m1-04-02
instruction: Select the headings below to learn more about prevalence.

_items.body:
The prevalence of Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus (T1DM) globally is rising quickly, especially in lower-income settings.
  • In 2025, 9.5 million people globally live with T1DM – this is an increase of 13% from 2021 data.

_graphic.alt: Digital glucometer with test strip and lancets

_items.body:
Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), accounting for more than 90 % of all diabetes cases, is the most common form of the disease.
  • Global data from 2021 shows that T2DM affected 506.0 million individuals, with 23.9 million new cases, 1.6 million deaths, and 75.3 million DALYs.
  • The global prevalence rates increased by 290.5 % from 1990.
  • Although men are more at risk of developing T2DM, women are more at risk of dying from T2DM‑related conditions.

_graphic.alt: Woman using a lancet pen to test her blood sugar

_items.body:
• 3.4 million adolescents globally live with T1DM, while 14.6 million live with T2DM.
  • Prevalence rates for T1DM are higher in female adolescents, while rates of T2DM are higher in adolescent males.

_graphic.alt: Blood glucose sensor on a child’s arm

title: Progression - T1DM
body:
T1DM is characterised by immune-mediated destruction of insulin-producing beta-cells in the pancreas.

T1D can be predicted months to years before the onset of symptomatic disease by the presence of islet autoantibodies in the blood.

_graphic.attribution: The Stages of Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus

title: c-m1-05-03
instruction: Drag the slider to reveal more information.

_items.title: Stage 1
_items.body: Stage 1: Detection of 2 or more islet autoantibodies with normal glucose tolerance.

_items.title: Stage 2
_items.body: Stage 2: 2 or more islet antibodies with abnormal glucose tolerance.

_items.title: Stage 3
_items.body: Stage 3: Clinical symptoms of hyperglycaemia (polyuria, polydipsia, unintentional weight loss) and the need for insulin replacement.

title: Progression - T2DM
body:
T2DM is also progressive in nature, characterised by a decline in beta-cell function and worsening of insulin resistance, leading to deteriorations in parameters including A1C, fasting plasma glucose (FPG), and postprandial glucose levels.

A decline in beta-cell function can begin as early as 12 years before diagnosis and continues throughout the disease process.

_graphic.attribution: Changing physiology and clinical complications in the natural history of type 2 diabetes

title: c-m1-05-05t
body:
Studies on the progression of pre-diabetes to overt disease observed that 8.1 % of subjects whose initial abnormal fasting glucose was 5.6-6.0 mmol/L and 24.3 % of subjects whose initial abnormal fasting glucose was 6.1-6.9 mmol/L developed diabetes over an average of 29.0 months.

As beta-cell function continues to decline, failure of monotherapy is also observed.

title: Obesity
body: Obesity is one of the most pressing global health crises of the 21<sup>st</sup> century, with its prevalence nearly tripling since 1975.

title: c-m1-06-02
instruction: Select the pictures below to learn more.

_items.backBody:
Obesity is a complex, chronic disease.

It goes beyond just a high BMI, it is marked by abnormal or excessive fat accumulation that adversely impacts health, elevating the risk of metabolic, cardiovascular, and musculoskeletal disorders.

Clinical obesity is diagnosed when excess adiposity directly impairs organ function or limits daily activities—for example, causing hypertension, obstructive sleep apnoea, or severe joint degeneration.
Pre-clinical obesity applies to individuals with excess fat accumulation but no overt complications, though they remain at elevated risk for future diseases.

title: Pathophysiology
body: The simple explanation of the development of obesity is a prolonged positive energy balance (more energy consumed than expended), but recent understanding has shown that mechanisms behind the condition are much more complicated.
instruction: Select the arrow to learn more.
mobileInstruction: Select the arrow to learn more.
_comment: setCompletionOn = inview | allItems

_items.body: Energy regulation involves a complex interaction between central regulatory pathways and multiple peripheral feedback signals arising from adipose and the gastrointestinal (GI) tract.

It is a dynamic process in which adjustments to one component of energy balance may elicit biological and/or behavioural ‘compensation’ in other components of the system.

These auto-regulatory or compensatory responses act to minimise disruptions to energy homoeostasis, and in turn, body weight.

Neurons trigger the release of peptides that stimulate melanocortin receptors (MC3 and MC4), which increases energy expenditure and decreases appetite.

This circuit is stimulated by adiposity and anorexigenic signals.
  • Peripheral signals related to energy stores are triggered by adipose tissue (leptin) and the pancreas (insulin).
  • Gut hormones with incretin-, hunger-, and satiety-stimulating effects, such as glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) improves the response of the pancreas to absorbed nutrients; GLP-1 reduce food intake centrally.
  • Secretin and cholecystokinin released from the gut inhibit appetite via the vagus nerve, which stimulate the brain.

When more energy is taken in than what can be stored in adipose tissue, fat molecules are stored in metabolically active cells, tissues, and organs (including skeletal muscle, heart, liver, kidney, pancreas, brain, and the intestinal tract).

_graphic.alt: Doctor holding a liver anatomy model

_items.body: Hence, the pathophysiology of obesity not only involves an increase in total body fat, especially in the intra-abdominal compartment in the presence of insulin resistance, but is also deposited into non-adipose tissues, especially in the liver, skeletal muscle, and the pancreas.

_graphic.alt: Integration of energy balance signals (appetite control)

title: Risk factors
body: Obesity arises from a complex interplay of genetic, environmental, behavioural, and socioeconomic factors that disrupt energy homeostasis, leading to sustained positive energy balance.
instruction: Select the headings below to learn more.
_comment: setCompletionOn = inview | allItems

_items.title: Genetics
_items.body: Twin and family studies estimate that 40 %-70 % of obesity risk is heritable. Interestingly, recent studies revealed that high genetic risk can be attenuated by healthy lifestyle factors.

_items.title: Ultra-processed diet
_items.body: Ultra-processed foods, which constitute >60 % of calories in high-income countries, are engineered to override satiety signals through high palatability and low fibre content.

_items.title: Physical inactivity
_items.body: Urbanisation reduced physical activity, with screen time displacing active pursuits.

_graphic.alt: Man lounging on a sofa with a remote control

_items.title: Sleep deprivation
_items.body: Sleep deprivation (<6 h/night) exacerbates metabolic dysregulation by elevating ghrelin (appetite-stimulating hormone) and reducing leptin (satiety hormone) levels.

_items.title: Endocrine-disrupting chemicals
_items.body: Disrupted endocrine system caused by certain chemicals found in products (e.g., phthalates), leading to disrupted insulin sensitivity or mimicking/blocking hormonal signalling.

_graphic.alt: Measuring a powder sample in a laboratory

_items.title: Gut microbiota disruption
_items.body: Disrupted gut microbiota disrupts energy harvest from food.

_items.title: Certain medications
_items.body: Certain medications, including antipsychotics, antidepressants, and glucocorticoids, promote weight gain through metabolic and appetitive effects.

_graphic.alt: Pills and capsules in a hand

title: Diagnostic factors
body:
BMI is a simplistic tool that has limitations; it cannot distinguish lean muscle mass from fat tissue.

It also overlooks fat distribution patterns; visceral fat, which surrounds internal organs and drives metabolic dysfunction, is a stronger predictor of disease risk than subcutaneous fat but remains invisible to BMI.

_items.backBody: ~30 % of those classified as obese with BMI only are metabolically healthy.
~20 % of people with normal BMI have high visceral fat and insulin resistance.

title: Epidemiology
body: 1 in 3 individuals globally are overweight/obese, regardless of countries’ economic status.
instruction: Select the headings below to learn more about the prevalence.

_items.body: Prevalence is higher in high-income countries (average of 60 %).
In 2021, global data shows 93.1 million individuals aged 5 years–14 years were overweight, and 80.6 million aged 15 years–24 years were obese.
Amongst this young age group, 11.2 % of individuals were overweight, while 6.9 % were regarded obese, with the latter rate being a 236.9 % increase in prevalence since 1990.
Obesity levels in individuals aged 5 years–14 years are estimated to increase to 15.6 % by 2050.

_graphic.alt: Doctor analysing healthcare data on a laptop

title: Complications
body: Obesity is not merely a cosmetic problem; it is a systemic disease that disrupts physiological equilibrium and affects nearly every organ system that culminate in life-threatening comorbidities mediated by chronic low-grade inflammation, hormonal dysregulation, oxidative stress, and ectopic fat deposition.
instruction: Select the headings below to learn more.Area of complicationClinical description

_items.body:
• Systemic insulin resistance, a hallmark of metabolic syndrome and T2DM.
  • Disrupted lipid metabolism leads to fat accumulation and glucose intolerance.
  • Conditions include non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) and cirrhosis.

• Hypertension is common due to increased blood volume, vasoconstriction and sodium retention.
  • Dyslipidaemia accelerates atherosclerosis, causing a 2–3-fold higher risk of coronary artery disease, heart failure, and stroke due to chronic inflammation and plaque instability.

• Respiratory function is mechanically compromised by restricting diaphragmatic movement, causing possible obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA), leading to oxidative stress and systemic inflammation.
  • Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS), characterised by chronic hypercapnia, increases mortality risk due to right heart failure and pulmonary hypertension.
• Accelerated glomerular hyperfiltration, proteinuria, and progressive renal decline; this risk is amplified by accompanying hypertension and diabetes.

• Excess weight on joints accelerates cartilage degradation, leading to osteoarthritis (OA).
  • Adipokines such as leptin and adiponectin exacerbate joint inflammation and synovial fibrosis.
  • Impaired fracture healing and increased osteoporosis risk due to chronic inflammation and vitamin D deficiency.

• Leptin resistance in the hypothalamus disrupts appetite regulation, perpetuating overeating.
  • Higher risk of depression and anxiety, mediated by inflammation-driven alterations in serotonin and dopamine signalling.
  • Neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s, are exacerbated by obesity-induced blood–brain barrier disruption and amyloid-beta accumulation.

• Hyperandrogenism and anovulation, contributing to polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and infertility.
  • In men, testosterone is converted to oestrogen, causing hypogonadism and reduced sperm quality.
  • Maternal obesity increases risks of gestational diabetes, preeclampsia, and congenital anomalies in offspring.

• State of chronic immune activation and dysfunction, impaired responses to pathogens with paradoxically increased autoimmune disease risk.
  • Impaired T-cell function and vaccine efficacy.

title: Treatment Options in Type 2 Diabetes (T2DM)
displayTitle: MOUNJAROTREATMENT OPTIONS IN TYPE 2 DIABETES (T2DM)
body: Goals of treatment in T2DM are to eliminate symptoms and slow or prevent complications.

title: c-m2-01-02
instruction: Select the picture below until you have seen all the information.

_items.body: Controlling hyperglycaemia and blood pressure minimise microvascular risk i.e. ocular and renal complications, neuropathy and metabolic risks.

Controlling lipids, hypertension and stopping smoking minimise macrovascular risk; i.e. focus on both managing blood glucose levels and managing additional comorbidities such as hypertension and dyslipidaemia.
T2DM may be managed with diet and exercise; some may require medication.
Oral antihyperglycaemic agents are the main class of medications, early therapy provides improved glycaemic control and reduced long-term complications.

Oral antihyperglycaemic medications may enhance pancreatic secretion of insulin (secretagogues), sensitise peripheral tissues to insulin (sensitisers), impair GI absorption of glucose or increase glycosuria (excretion of sugar in the urine).

title: c-m2-01-03
body: Combinations with different mechanisms of action could be synergistic to provide the best therapeutic effect; insulin is usually added if >3 agents fail to manage blood glucose levels.
instruction: Select the headings below to learn more.Class of agentDescription

_items.body:
• Insulin secretagogues; stimulate release of insulin from the pancreatic beta cells, improve peripheral and hepatic insulin sensitivity.
  • 1st generation agents less utilised due to tendency to cause side effects; 2nd generation agents (glyburide, glipizide and glimepiride) can be given at low doses, once daily.
  • Can be used as monotherapy or in combination with other oral agents or insulin; promote weight gain, usually of 2 kg –5 kg, most common side effect is hypoglycaemia.

• Short acting secretagogues, initiate insulin secretion more so during mealtimes than sulfonylureas to reduce post-prandial hyperglycaemia (e.g. repaglinide and nateglinide).
  • Some weight gain but lower risk of hypoglycaemia; can be used as monotherapy, useful in those who cannot tolerate sulfonylureas.

• Peripheral insulin sensitisers; decreases hepatic glucose production (gluconeogenesis) and gastrointestinal absorption of glucose; insulin sensitivity is improved due to increased peripheral glucose uptake and use, lowering basal and post-prandial glucose levels. Lowers lipid levels and decreases levels of plasminogen activator inhibitor 1 i.e. an antithrombotic effect.
  • Metformin the only biguanide available for use clinically in many countries, as 1st line oral therapy for T2DM; no weight gain; weight loss due to suppressed appetite; rarely causes hypoglycaemia; safe to use in combination with other drugs and insulin.
  • GI AEs are common (dyspepsia and diarrhoea), which subside over time for most; rarely causes vitamin B12 malabsorption. Can cause life-threatening lactic acidosis (rare); avoid in those at risk of acidaemia (e.g. renal insufficiency, hypoxia, metabolic acidosis or dehydration) and surgery, IV contrast or severe illness.

• Insulin sensitisers; need insulin to be present and usage of 12 – 16 weeks to reach optimal efficacy; decrease peripheral insulin resistance; bind a nuclear receptor in lipid cells involved in transcription of genes that regulate glucose and lipid metabolism. They lower triglyceride levels, increase HDL levels, with anti-inflammatory and anti-atherosclerotic effects (e.g. pioglitazone and rosiglitazone).
  • Used as monotherapy or in combination with sulfonylureas, metformin, meglitinide, DPP-4 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists or insulin; only agents proven to slow disease progression, especially in early disease.
  • Currently available agents are not hepatotoxic; liver function should be monitored. Can cause peripheral oedema especially with insulin, substantial weight gain (>10 kg); increased risk of CV conditions and fracture.

• Delay the absorption of glucose and prevent post-prandial glucose spikes by prolonging absorption of carbohydrates (acarbose and miglitol); less effective at reducing blood glucose levels than other oral agents.
  • Can cause flatulence, introduce slowly to prevent GI disturbances; used in combination with other agents and insulin.

• Prolong the action of incretin hormone and prolong the action of glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) by inhibiting the enzyme DPP-4, which is involved in the breakdown of GLP-1 (sitagliptin, saxagliptin and linagliptin).
  • Can be used as monotherapy or combined with metformin or TZDs. They are weight neutral.

• Inhibit SGLT2 in the proximal tubule of the kidney, blocks the reabsorption of glucose causing glycosuria (excretion of glucose in the urine); include canagliflozin, dapagliflozin and empagliflozin.
  • May cause some weight loss and lower blood pressure.
  • A common side effect is genitourinary infection, particularly mycotic infection; patients may also experience orthostatic symptoms.

• Adjunct to exercise and diet to improve glycaemic control (e.g. bromocriptine); act on central dopamine-2 receptors and affect circadian neuronal activities and reset an abnormally elevated drive for increased plasma glucose, triglyceride, and free fatty acid levels in fasting and postprandial states in insulin-resistant patients.
  • Less often used due to GI side effects and possible orthostatic effects and syncope.

• Mimic physiologically normal insulin levels; patients may become insulinopenic (insulin is only effective therapy), while most T2DM patients have insulin resistance, so small changes in insulin dosage will not make a difference to glycaemia.

• Enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion and slow gastric emptying, mimic endogenous incretin GLP-1 (e.g. semaglutide, exenatide, liraglutide, albiglutide and dulaglutide); may promote beta cell proliferation. Reduce appetite and help with weight loss.
  • Taken once or twice daily, or weekly as required; can be combined with metformin or sulfonylureas; common GI AEs especially nausea and vomiting, may slightly increase the risk of pancreatitis.

• Dual incretin agonist; receptor agonist for GIP and GLP-1 receptors; increase glucose-dependent secretion of insulin, decreases glucagon secretion, slows gastric emptying; decreases appetite and induces weight loss (tirzepatide).
  • Can be used as adjunct to lifestyle modifications.

• Pancreatic beta-cell hormone; helps regulate post-prandial glucose levels (pramlintide); mimics the action of amylin and suppresses post-prandial glucagon secretion, slows gastric emptying and promotes satiety.
  • Used in combination with mealtime insulin.

title: c-m2-04-03
body: Below is a summary of a few of the more recent guidelines that provide the latest recommendations.
instruction: Select the headings below to learn more.
_comment: setCompletionOn = inview | allItems

_items.title: ADA Pharmacologic Treatment of Obesity in Adults: Standards of Care in Overweight and Obesity (2026)
_items.body:
• Obesity medications are recommended with lifestyle therapy.
  • Treatment goals: ≥5 % weight loss for health benefits, ≥10 % –15 % for disease modification (e.g., HFpEF, MASH, OSA).
  • In adults with overweight or obesity and T2DM, BP, OSA, MASH, and ASCVD, GLP-1 agonists or dual GLP-1/GIP agonists are preferred.
  • Tirzepatide: placebo‑subtracted weight loss ~16.2 %, with demonstrated benefit in T2D, BP, OSA, MASH, and ASCVD.
  • Semaglutide: ~11.9 % weight loss, strong evidence for T2D remission and CV benefit.

_items.title: NICE Guideline Overweight and obesity management (2026)
_items.body:
• After dietary, exercise and behavioural approaches have been started and evaluated, weight management medicines should be initiated.
  • Tirzepatide, semaglutide, liraglutide and orlistat are recommended weight management medicines.

_items.title: AACE Consensus Statement (2025)
_items.body:
• Medications preferred based on complication‑centric care.
  • Tirzepatide and semaglutide prioritised for cardiometabolic complications (T2D, ASCVD, HFpEF, MASH) and biomechanical complications (tirzepatide or phentermine/topiramate in OSA, semaglutide in OA).

_items.title: EASO. A new framework for the diagnosis, staging and management of obesity in adults (2024) & EASO Obesity Management Algorithm
_items.body:
• Foundation of care is lifestyle modifications.
  • Medication should be tailored to comorbidities:
    • T2DM – tirzepatide, semaglutide.
    • CVD – semaglutide (for MACE reduction).
    • HF – tirzepatide, semaglutide.
    • Prediabetes – tirzepatide, semaglutide, liraglutide, orlistat.
    • Liver disease (MASH) – tirzepatide.
    • Sleep apnoea – tirzepatide.
    • Knee osteoarthritis – semaglutide.
  • Other agents (orlistat, naltrexone/bupropion, phentermine/topiramate, liraglutide) noted but less effective for weight loss.

title: Indication
body: Tirzepatide is indicated for Type 2 diabetes mellitus and weight management.
instruction: Select the headings below to learn more.

_items.body:
Tirzepatide is indicated for the treatment of adults with insufficiently controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus as an adjunct to diet and exercise:
  • as monotherapy when metformin is considered inappropriate due to intolerance or contraindications.
  • in addition to other medicinal products for the treatment of diabetes.
See local product leaflet for study results with respect to combinations, effects on glycaemic control and the populations studied.

The safety and efficacy of MOUNJARO in children aged less than 18 years have not yet been established.

Tirzepatide is indicated as an adjunct to a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity for weight management, including weight loss and weight maintenance, in adults with an initial Body Mass Index (BMI) of
  • ≥30 kg/m2 (obesity) or
  • ≥27 kg/m2 to <30 kg/m2 (overweight) in the presence of at least one weight-related comorbid condition (e.g., hypertension, dyslipidaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea, cardiovascular disease, prediabetes, or type 2 diabetes mellitus).
See local product leaflet for trial results with respect to obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF).

_graphic.attribution: Mechanism of action of GLP-1 RA and dual GIP/GLP-1 agonists.

_items.title: The incretin effect
_items.body: The incretin effect is when oral glucose, absorbed from the gut, leads to the stimulated secretion of both GIP and GLP-1 hormones, which in turn provides a stimulus to β-cells in the islets of Langerhans to augment their insulin secretory responses. Reductions in the incretin effect usually are associated with impairments in oral glucose tolerance (impaired glucose tolerance or diabetes).

_items.title: Tirzepatide
_items.body: Tirzepatide is a long-acting GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist, highly selective to human GIP and GLP-1 receptors, with a high affinity to both receptors. The activity of tirzepatide on the GIP receptor is similar to native GIP hormone; the activity of tirzepatide on the GLP-1 receptor is lower compared to native GLP-1 hormone.

_items.title: Receptors
_items.body: GIP receptors and GLP-1 receptors can be found in the pancreas (islets of Langerhans), in the brain, heart and blood vessels, immune cells and adipose tissue, where GIP and GLP-1 exert biological activities.

_items.title: Appetite and food intake
_items.body: Tirzepatide distributes to and activates neurons in brain regions involved in regulation of appetite and food intake.

_items.title: Fat utilisation
_items.body:
• Animal studies show that tirzepatide can modulate fat utilisation through the GIP receptor.
  • In human adipocytes cultured in vitro, tirzepatide acts on GIP receptors to regulate glucose uptake and modulate lipid uptake and lipolysis.

_items.title: Note

_items.title: Design
_items.body: International, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial; 52 weeks.

_items.title: Comparator
_items.body: Tirzepatide MTD or placebo.

_items.title: Patient population
_items.body: Adults with HFpEF and BMI ≥30 (n=731).

title: Outcomes
body:
• Tirzepatide reduced the risk of worsening heart failure assessed as the composite of cardiovascular death or heart failure event, defined as heart failure hospitalisation, urgent heart failure visits, or oral diuretic intensification for worsening heart failure.
  • Adjudicated death from cardiovascular causes or a worsening heart-failure event occurred in 9.9 % in tirzepatide patients and in 15.3 % in placebo patients (HR 0.62; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.41 to 0.95; P=0.026).
  • Tirzepatide resulted in a statistically significant improvement in heart failure symptoms and physical limitations compared with placebo, as assessed by the KCCQ-CSS.

_items.body: Consistent A1c lowering of ~2.0–2.6 %, superior to placebo, basal/prandial insulin, and semaglutide.

_items.title: Supporting study(ies)
_items.body: SURPASS‑1 (Rosenstock, 2021); SURPASS‑2 (Frías, 2021); SURPASS‑3 (Ludvik, 2021); SURPASS‑4 (Del Prato, 2021); SURPASS‑5 (Dahl, 2022); SURPASS‑6 (Rosenstock, 2023)

_items.title: Outcome
_items.body: Dose‑dependent reductions: ~7–12 kg in adults, 7 % – 11 % BMI reduction in adolescents. Superior to insulin and semaglutide.

_items.title: Supporting study(ies)
_items.body: SURPASS‑1; SURPASS‑2; SURPASS‑3; SURPASS‑4; SURPASS‑5; SURPASS‑6; SURPASS‑PEDS

_items.title: Outcome
_items.body: 80 % – 97 % achieved A1c <7 %; up to 62 % achieved A1c <5.7 %.

_items.title: Supporting study(ies)
_items.body: SURPASS‑1; SURPASS‑2; SURPASS‑3; SURPASS‑4; SURPASS‑5; SURPASS‑6

_items.title: Outcome
_items.body: Lower rates of hypoglycaemia compared with insulin comparators (1 % – 3 % vs 16 % – 19 %).

_items.title: Supporting study(ies)
_items.body: SURPASS‑3; SURPASS‑4; SURPASS‑6

_items.title: Outcome
_items.body: No excess CV risk; hazard ratio for MACE ~0.74 vs glargine (SURPASS‑4); noninferior to dulaglutide in CVOT.

_items.body: SURPASS‑4 (Del Prato, 2021); SURPASS‑CVOT (Nicholls, 2025)

_items.title: Outcome

_items.title: Supporting study(ies)

_items.title: Outcome
_items.body: Improvements in fasting glucose, lipids, blood pressure, and waist circumference.

_items.title: Supporting study(ies)
_items.body: SURPASS‑2; SURPASS‑3; SURPASS‑4

_items.title: Outcome
_items.body: A1c reduction of ~2.2 %, BMI reduction up to 11 %, safety profile consistent with adults.

_items.title: Supporting study(ies)
